title: A Nostalgic Look at Crayons
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with personal banter about Hurricane Irma's impact on Atlanta, a power outage, and the loss of a family pet cat. They then turn to crayons: the nostalgia of Crayola, the Yale-cited smell recognition finding, and batik and encaustic (wax-based) art as precursors. The history covers the conté crayon, early beeswax crayons by Lemercier and J.S. Staedtler, the coal-mining byproduct sarasin and Offenheim and Ziffa, paraffin wax and Charles Bowley (Bolley) producing round crayons after the Civil War, and the link to kindergarten and industrial-era schooling. Binney and Smith, Alice Binney's role, the non-toxic redesign, and the rename to Crayola follow. The episode covers Crayola color naming, retired colors (Indian Red, flesh, Prussian blue), the giant crayon, a survey of favorite colors, and the new blue "Blutiful" from Oregon State researchers. The episode closes with a listener mail about a Satanism episode.

segments.title: Hurricane Irma and pet loss banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck talk about Hurricane Irma's effects on Atlanta, including fallen trees and a three-day power outage, and the death of a family cat. They also note Jerry is absent and mention the crayon topic.

segments.title: Crayon nostalgia and Crayola's smell recognition
segments.summary: The hosts discuss nostalgia for Crayola crayons and a Yale study that ranked the crayon smell as highly recognizable to adults. They also talk about the Crayola name and the brand's dominance over Prang.

segments.title: Batik and early wax art
segments.summary: Chuck recounts doing batik as a child in an elementary school program and making Herschel Walker canvases. They explain batik as a wax-resist dyeing method and note that wax-based art predates crayons by thousands of years.

segments.title: Encaustic art and conté crayon origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss encaustic art, which mixes pigment and melted wax. They explain that the conté crayon grew out of chalk-based pastels, and that early content crayons were beeswax and came in black, brown, and red.

segments.title: Early manufactured wax crayons
segments.summary: Joseph Lemercier produced wax crayons by the 1820s, and J.S. Staedtler later sold crayons encased in wood in Germany. Beeswax was hard to work with, which led to later changes.

segments.title: Coal byproducts, paraffin, and round crayons
segments.summary: Coal mining in Eastern Europe produced sarasin, a softer and cheaper wax used by Offenheim and Ziffa. Later, Charles Bowley Bolley used paraffin, a petroleum byproduct, to make the first round crayons recognizable today, around the Civil War. The hosts also tie this to industrialization and the rise of schooling.

segments.title: Binney and Smith, Crayola's origins, and kindergarten
segments.summary: Binney and Smith made pigments and used crayons to mark shipments. Alice Binney, a teacher, suggested they manufacture crayons, and they made them non-toxic, creating Crayola in the 1880s. The hosts discuss schooling expansion and the government purchase for Native American schools.

segments.title: Crayola color names, retired colors, and the Blutiful blue
segments.summary: Crayola took over Mondral's crayon division and adopted its names and pigments, then renamed colors for kids. Flesh, Indian Red, and Prussian blue were retired. The hosts cover favorite colors, the giant crayon, and a new blue from Oregon State researchers named Blutiful.

segments.title: Listener mail on Satanism episode
segments.summary: Hosts read a listener email from a Christian pastor who said the Church of Satan episode deepened his understanding of other belief systems. Josh and Chuck close with social media links.
